claim: The golden mimicry complex consists of at least 140 different putative mimics from four arthropod orders including ants, wasps, bugs, tree hoppers and spiders.
source: Here, we report a new multi-order mimicry complex that includes at least 140 different putative mimics from four arthropod orders including ants, wasps, bugs, tree hoppers and spiders.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 which lists the species, and is stated in the abstract.

claim: All members of the golden mimicry complex are characterised by a conspicuous golden body and an ant Gestalt.
source: All members of this mimicry complex are characterised by a conspicuous golden body and an ant Gestalt, but vary substantially in their defensive traits.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations and measurements described in the methods and results sections.

claim: Members of the golden mimicry complex vary substantially in their defensive traits.
source: All members of this mimicry complex are characterised by a conspicuous golden body and an ant Gestalt, but vary substantially in their defensive traits.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of defensive traits presented in Table 3 and Figure 4A.

claim: Mimics in the golden complex were similarly effective at deterring predators even when mildly defended.
source: However, they were similarly effective at deterring predators - even mildly defended mimics were rarely eaten by a community of invertebrate and vertebrate predators both in the wild and during staged trials.
evidence: The claim is supported by predation data from field studies (Table 2) and experimental trials (Figure 6).

claim: The three predatory guilds avoid the mimics because of the additive influence of the various defensive traits.
source: We propose that despite the predominance of less defended mimics the three predatory guilds avoid the mimics because of the additive influence of the various defensive traits.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental results showing similar protection across mimics with varying defenses.

claim: Classic Müllerian mimicry was thought to only include equally defended species.
source: Classic Müllerian mimicry was thought to only include equally defended species (Müller, 1878), while Batesian mimicry (Bates, 1862) describes undefended species resembling defended models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Müller, 1878.

claim: Batesian mimicry describes undefended species resembling defended models.
source: Classic Müllerian mimicry was thought to only include equally defended species (Müller, 1878), while Batesian mimicry (Bates, 1862) describes undefended species resembling defended models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bates, 1862.

claim: The dichotomy between Müllerian and Batesian mimicry represents the end-points of a mimetic spectrum that contains species that vary in their mimetic fidelity and/or their degree of defensiveness.
source: In reality, this simplistic dichotomy (sensu Speed, 1999) represents the end-points of a mimetic spectrum that contains species that vary in their mimetic fidelity and/or their degree of defensiveness.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Speed, 1999.

claim: Discrepancy in protection between two mimetic species may dilute the protection of a more defended species.
source: Discrepancy in protection between two mimetic species may dilute the protection of a more defended species (Speed, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Speed, 1999.

claim: Great tits attacked artificial models more often when less defended mimics were frequently encountered and food was restricted.
source: Great tits (Parus major, Paridae, Passeriformes) for instance, attacked artificial models more often when less defended mimics were frequently encountered and food was restricted (Rowland et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rowland et al., 2010.

claim: Wild caught great tits equally avoided four species of true bugs with varying levels of defence but which shared similar warning colours.
source: wild caught great tits equally avoided four species of true bugs with varying levels of defence but which shared similar warning colours (Hodová Svádová et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hodová Svádová et al., 2013.

claim: Müllerian mimicry rings typically consist of a few closely related species.
source: Müllerian mimicry rings typically consist of a few closely related species (Symula et al., 2001; Williams, 2007; Alexandrou et al., 2011), with the exceptions of the species-rich mutillid wasp (Wilson et al., 2012, 2015), Heliconius butterfly (Mallet and Gilbert, 1995) and bumblebee (Williams, 2007) complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Symula et al., 2001; Williams, 2007; Alexandrou et al., 2011.

claim: The mutillid wasp complex is suspected of including species from other orders but this has not been formally presented.
source: The mutillid wasp complex is suspected of including species from other orders but this has not been formally presented (Wilson et al., 2012, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wilson et al., 2012, 2015.

claim: A mathematical model suggests that mimicry complexes should be common in multispecies communities with distantly related taxa.
source: A mathematical model suggests that mimicry complexes should be common in multispecies communities with distantly related taxa (Beatty et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Beatty et al., 2004.

claim: Ants have been largely overlooked as Müllerian mimics.
source: For example, ants have been largely overlooked as Müllerian mimics, yet they are diverse, typically well defended through a range of defensive measures including a sting, noxious chemicals, spines, a thickened cuticle, mandibles and communal attack (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature and the authors' observations.

claim: Ants are diverse and typically well defended through a range of defensive measures including a sting, noxious chemicals, spines, a thickened cuticle, mandibles and communal attack.
source: For example, ants have been largely overlooked as Müllerian mimics, yet they are diverse, typically well defended through a range of defensive measures including a sting, noxious chemicals, spines, a thickened cuticle, mandibles and communal attack (Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990.

claim: Species within Müllerian rings use the same defensive traits.
source: Species within Müllerian rings thus far described use the same defensive traits.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from the literature on mimicry rings.

claim: Heliconius butterflies rely on their distastefulness.
source: Heliconius butterflies, for instance, rely on their distastefulness while mutillid wasps have a venomous sting.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Heliconius butterflies.

claim: Mutillid wasps have a venomous sting.
source: Heliconius butterflies, for instance, rely on their distastefulness while mutillid wasps have a venomous sting.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mutillid wasps.

claim: The degree of distastefulness or level of venom toxicity within a mimicry ring is expected to vary among members.
source: The degree of distastefulness or level of venom toxicity within a mimicry ring is expected to vary among members.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical expectations from mimicry theory.

claim: Most environments contain a wide range of potential predators of mimics.
source: Experimental investigations, that started a hundred years ago (e.g. McAtee, 1912, 1932), have tended to focus on a single visually-oriented predatory guild and yet most environments contain a wide range of potential predators of mimics.
evidence: The claim is based on general ecological knowledge.

claim: Species that mimic ants may encounter several ant-averse and ant-eating predators.
source: For example, species that mimic ants may encounter several ant-averse and ant-eating predators (Pekár et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pekár et al., 2011.

claim: In leaf litter microhabitats, ant-eating predators and ant-adverse nonvisually-orienting predators are more common than visually-orienting ones.
source: In some microhabitats, such as leaf litter, the ant-eating predators (which often use chemical cues to recognise prey) and ant-adverse nonvisually-orienting predators are indeed more common than visually-orienting ones, thus exerting strong selection pressure on mimics to signal their unpalatability in sensory modalities other than visual.
evidence: The claim is based on ecological knowledge about predator distributions.

claim: The golden mimicry complex includes 126 ant species, seven spider species, three species of true bugs, one mutillid wasp and one treehopper.
source: We uncovered a cross-order mimicry complex, consisting of at least 140 arthropod species including 126 ant species, seven spider species (and several forms), three species of true bugs, one mutillid wasp and one treehopper (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Members of the golden complex are all ant-like in appearance and characterised by a dorsal patch of golden coloration combined with blackish colouration.
source: Members of the complex are all ant-like in appearance and characterised by a dorsal patch of golden coloration combined with blackish colouration (Figure 1, Video 1), which we recognise as an aposematic signal (RGB contrast: mean = 241.4, SD = 58.1, N = 55).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observations documented in Figure 1 and Video 1, and by RGB contrast measurements.

claim: The RGB contrast of the golden/black coloration in the complex has a mean of 241.4 (SD = 58.1, N = 55).
source: Members of the complex are all ant-like in appearance and characterised by a dorsal patch of golden coloration combined with blackish colouration (Figure 1, Video 1), which we recognise as an aposematic signal (RGB contrast: mean = 241.4, SD = 58.1, N = 55).
evidence: The claim is supported by RGB contrast measurements.

claim: Related non-mimetic species are typically uniformly black or brown.
source: Related non-mimetic species are typically uniformly black or brown.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of related species.

claim: Among hymenopteran representatives (ants and wasps), the golden sheen is generated only by pubescence of varying density.
source: Among the hymenopteran representatives (ants and wasps), the golden sheen is generated only by pubescence of varying density (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by SEM observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: The golden visual effect in hymenopterans entirely disappears when they are submerged in ethanol.
source: Consequently, this visual effect entirely disappears when they are submerged in ethanol.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: True bugs and spiders use a combination of hairs and yellow pigmentation to achieve the golden sheen.
source: In contrast, true bugs and spiders use a combination of hairs and yellow pigmentation (in the exocuticle of the abdomen/gaster), while the treehopper appears to use only pigment as the golden shine is lost after death.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations described in the methods and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The treehopper appears to use only pigment to achieve the golden sheen as the golden shine is lost after death.
source: In contrast, true bugs and spiders use a combination of hairs and yellow pigmentation (in the exocuticle of the abdomen/gaster), while the treehopper appears to use only pigment as the golden shine is lost after death.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of color changes after death.

claim: Cluster analysis suggested the existence of ten putative rings within the complex according to variation in the dorsal colour pattern.
source: The cluster analysis suggested the existence of ten putative rings within the complex, according to variation in the dorsal colour pattern but the differences were rather small (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The differences between the ten putative rings were rather small.
source: The cluster analysis suggested the existence of ten putative rings within the complex, according to variation in the dorsal colour pattern but the differences were rather small (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on the cluster analysis results.

claim: The putative rings were distributed across the Australian continent with a considerable overlap.
source: These rings were distributed across the Australian continent with a considerable overlap.
evidence: The claim is supported by distribution data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Rings in the east coast of Australia overlapped where species richness was the greatest.
source: For instance, rings in the east coast of Australia overlapped where species richness was the greatest (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the distribution map in Figure 3B.

claim: The degree of sympatry in a ring was not related to colour pattern similarity.
source: However, the degree of sympatry in a ring was not related to colour pattern (estimated from 24 measures of the colour pattern, body size and area of golden patch) similarity (Mantel test, r = −0.03, p=0.79).
evidence: The claim is supported by Mantel test results (r = −0.03, p=0.79).

claim: There was no strong effect of phylogeny on the classification into rings.
source: We did not find a strong effect of phylogeny on the classification into rings (GLS, Pagel's λ = 0.22, Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GLS analysis with Pagel's λ = 0.22.

claim: The splitting into ten putative rings was artificial and there is only one complex.
source: All this indicates that the splitting into ten putative rings was artificial and there is only one complex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the statistical analyses showing no relationship between sympatry and color pattern, and weak phylogenetic signal.

claim: The unpalatability of 100 species belonging to the golden mimicry complex was determined.
source: We determined the unpalatability of 100 species belonging to the golden mimicry complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods and results describing unpalatability measurements.

claim: Total unpalatability for each mimic was estimated based on the sum of morphological, chemical, and behavioural defensive traits.
source: Because several complementary forms of defence are likely, we estimated total unpalatability for each mimic based on the sum of morphological, chemical, and behavioural defensive traits.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used to estimate unpalatability.

claim: The analyses uncovered a spectrum of mimics from non-defended (Batesian) to highly defended (Müllerian) species.
source: Our analyses uncovered a spectrum of mimics from non-defended (Batesian) to highly defended (Müllerian) species.
evidence: The claim is supported by the unpalatability measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The spider and treehopper species had the lowest unpalatability score and were classified as Batesian mimics.
source: For instance, the spider and treehopper species had the lowest unpalatability score (i.e. sum of normalised measurements on defensive traits) and were therefore classified as Batesian mimics.
evidence: The claim is based on unpalatability measurements.

claim: Daerlac bugs, mutillid wasps and all ant species were unpalatable with considerable variation in the degree of unpalatability.
source: Daerlac bugs, mutillid wasps and all ant species were unpalatable, but we found considerable variation in the degree of unpalatability ranging from quasi-Müllerian to unambiguously Müllerian, mimics.
evidence: The claim is based on unpalatability measurements.

claim: The index of unpalatability had an overall normal distribution.
source: The index of unpalatability had an overall normal distribution (Shapiro-Wilk normality test, W = 0.98, p=0.21) with the highest frequency consisting of moderately-palatable species.
evidence: The claim is supported by Shapiro-Wilk normality test (W = 0.98, p=0.21).

claim: The highest frequency of unpalatability consisted of moderately-palatable species.
source: The index of unpalatability had an overall normal distribution (Shapiro-Wilk normality test, W = 0.98, p=0.21) with the highest frequency consisting of moderately-palatable species.
evidence: The claim is supported by the distribution shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Unpalatability varied in each ring but the variation was not significantly different among the ten rings.
source: Unpalatability varied in each ring but the variation was not significantly different among the ten rings suggested previously (Bartlett test, K26 = 11, p=0.09, Figure 4A) supporting further the existence of only one complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by Bartlett test (K26 = 11, p=0.09).

claim: The absolute area of the golden colouration increased with unpalatability.
source: We discovered that the absolute area of the golden colouration increased with unpalatability (controlling for the effect of phylogeny and body size: GLS, F1,91 = 21.1, p<0.0001, Figure 4B) supporting the hypothesis that the golden colour is an aposematic signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by GLS analysis (F1,91 = 21.1, p<0.0001) and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The positive relationship between golden coloration area and unpalatability supports the hypothesis that the golden colour is an aposematic signal.
source: We discovered that the absolute area of the golden colouration increased with unpalatability (controlling for the effect of phylogeny and body size: GLS, F1,91 = 21.1, p<0.0001, Figure 4B) supporting the hypothesis that the golden colour is an aposematic signal.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the statistical relationship between color and unpalatability.

claim: Predation of mimics was quantified by the 12 most abundant predatory species that co-occurred with 13 sympatric mimetic species.
source: We quantified predation of mimics by the 12 most abundant predatory species that co-occurred with 13 sympatric mimetic species belonging to the complex (Table 2).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental design and is supported by data in Table 2.

claim: Gut content or faeces of 553 spiders, 50 skinks, and 48 birds were analyzed using Next Generation Sequencing.
source: We analysed gut content or faeces of these predators (553 spiders, 50 skinks, and 48 birds), representing three different guilds, using Next Generation Sequencing, which allows identification of prey to species.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Individuals of all predatory species were positive for primers targeting the DNA of ants, spiders, and mutillid wasps.
source: We found that individuals of all predatory species were positive for primers targeting the DNA of ants, spiders, and mutillid wasps.
evidence: The claim is supported by NGS results.

claim: The frequency of captured mimics was not significantly different from their availability in the environment.
source: The frequency of captured mimics was not significantly different from their availability in the environment (X212 = 1.5, p=0.99) because mimics were very rare in the field.
evidence: The claim is supported by Chi-square test (X212 = 1.5, p=0.99).

claim: Only three mimetic species (Camponotus aeneopilosus, Myrmarachne erythrocephala, Myrmarachne luctuosa) were detected in the faeces/gut of predators.
source: Only three mimetic species (Camponotus aeneopilosus, Myrmarachne erythrocephala, Myrmarachne luctuosa) were detected in the faeces/gut of predators.
evidence: The claim is supported by NGS data presented in Table 2.

claim: Visually-oriented and non-visually oriented euryphagous predators captured mimics at less than 4% frequency.
source: Visually-oriented and non-visually oriented euryphagous (ant-adverse) predators captured mimics at less than 4% frequency, whereas specialized ant-eating predators captured mostly Batesian mimics (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 2.

claim: Specialized ant-eating predators captured mostly Batesian mimics.
source: Visually-oriented and non-visually oriented euryphagous (ant-adverse) predators captured mimics at less than 4% frequency, whereas specialized ant-eating predators captured mostly Batesian mimics (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Table 2.

claim: The overall attack rate estimated for all predators was marginally significantly negatively related to the unpalatability of mimics when it included two Batesian mimics.
source: The overall attack rate estimated for all predators was marginally significantly negatively related to the unpalatability of mimics when it included two Batesian mimics (GAM, F3.8,4.6 = 3.8, p=0.045, Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GAM analysis (F3.8,4.6 = 3.8, p=0.045) and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Eastern water skinks captured non-mimetic spiders at significantly higher frequency than members of the mimetic complex.
source: Eastern water skinks (N = 26) are visually-oriented generalist predators and captured (i.e. ate) non-mimetic spiders at significantly higher frequency than members of the mimetic complex such as ants, spiders and bugs (GEE-b, X25 = 125.8, p<0.0001, Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by GEE-b analysis (X25 = 125.8, p<0.0001) and shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was a strong positive relationship between prey unpalatability and the post-attack response of skinks.
source: In accordance with our classification of unpalatability, we found a strong positive relationship between prey unpalatability and the post-attack response of skinks (GLM, F1,4 = 19.4, p=0.012, Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GLM analysis (F1,4 = 19.4, p=0.012) and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mimic or non-mimic spiders were immediately eaten by skinks.
source: Mimic or non-mimic spiders were immediately eaten, but skinks showed an adverse response to mimic ants and bugs.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from predation trials.

claim: Skinks showed an adverse response to mimic ants and bugs.
source: Mimic or non-mimic spiders were immediately eaten, but skinks showed an adverse response to mimic ants and bugs.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from predation trials.

claim: Mimic ants and bugs were clearly distasteful because the skinks immediately cleaned their mouths and frequently spat the prey out.
source: These prey were clearly distasteful because the skinks immediately cleaned their mouths and frequently spat the prey out.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral observations during predation trials.

claim: Non-visually oriented ant-adverse Lampona spiders captured non-mimic spiders significantly more frequently than all mimics.
source: We found similar patterns in the non-visually oriented ant-adverse Lampona spiders (N = 25), which captured non-mimic spiders significantly more frequently than all mimics (Cochran test, X25 = 104, p<0.0001, Figure 6), showing no differentiation between the mimics.
evidence: The claim is supported by Cochran test (X25 = 104, p<0.0001) and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Lampona spiders showed no differentiation between the mimics.
source: We found similar patterns in the non-visually oriented ant-adverse Lampona spiders (N = 25), which captured non-mimic spiders significantly more frequently than all mimics (Cochran test, X25 = 104, p<0.0001, Figure 6), showing no differentiation between the mimics.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of predation trials.

claim: Visually oriented ant-eating specialist Servaea spiders readily attacked and captured mimics as well as non-mimics.
source: By contrast, the visually oriented ant-eating specialist Servaea spiders (N = 27) readily attacked and captured mimics as well as non-mimics.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from predation trials.

claim: Servaea spiders appeared to differentiate between mimics' levels of defence.
source: Although these spiders readily attacked the mimics they did appear to differentiate between their levels of defence (attack: GEE-b, X24 = 15763, p<0.0001, Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by GEE-b analysis (X24 = 15763, p<0.0001) and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The most unpalatable ant was attacked at a significantly lower frequency than other mimics by Servaea spiders.
source: The most unpalatable ant was attacked at a significantly lower frequency than other mimics (contrasts, p<0.008) and moderately unpalatable ant species were captured at a significantly lower frequency than bug and spider mimics (contrasts, p<0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by contrast tests (p<0.008).

claim: Moderately unpalatable ant species were captured at a significantly lower frequency than bug and spider mimics by Servaea spiders.
source: The most unpalatable ant was attacked at a significantly lower frequency than other mimics (contrasts, p<0.008) and moderately unpalatable ant species were captured at a significantly lower frequency than bug and spider mimics (contrasts, p<0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by contrast tests (p<0.006).

claim: Euryphagous and ant-adverse predators were less likely to capture a mimic than a non-mimic.
source: In summary, euryphagous and ant-adverse predators were less likely to capture a mimic than a non-mimic while the ant-specialist attacked the ants and ant-mimics alike but the likelihood of attack varied according to the mimic's actual unpalatability.
evidence: The claim summarizes the results from predation trials.

claim: The ant-specialist attacked the ants and ant-mimics alike but the likelihood of attack varied according to the mimic's actual unpalatability.
source: In summary, euryphagous and ant-adverse predators were less likely to capture a mimic than a non-mimic while the ant-specialist attacked the ants and ant-mimics alike but the likelihood of attack varied according to the mimic's actual unpalatability.
evidence: The claim summarizes the results from predation trials.

claim: There was no relationship between levels of unpalatability and the sum of predation pressure exerted by the three predatory guilds.
source: There was no relationship between levels of unpalatability and the sum of predation pressure (K-values) exerted by the three predatory guilds (LM, F1,3 = 1.83, p=0.27, Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LM analysis (F1,3 = 1.83, p=0.27) and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The species richness of the golden complex exceeds those of fish or millipedes.
source: The species richness of this golden complex exceeds those of fish or millipedes (Marek and Bond, 2009; Alexandrou et al., 2011) but is currently smaller than in mutillid wasp (Wilson et al., 2012, 2015), heliconid butterfly (Mallet and Gilbert, 1995) and bumblebee (Williams, 2007) complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: The golden complex is currently smaller than mutillid wasp, heliconid butterfly and bumblebee complexes.
source: The species richness of this golden complex exceeds those of fish or millipedes (Marek and Bond, 2009; Alexandrou et al., 2011) but is currently smaller than in mutillid wasp (Wilson et al., 2012, 2015), heliconid butterfly (Mallet and Gilbert, 1995) and bumblebee (Williams, 2007) complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: The key members in the golden complex are ants.
source: The key members in the golden complex are ants but the complex is taxonomically broad and includes species with distant phylogenetic origins.
evidence: The claim is based on the composition data showing 126 ant species out of 140 total species.

claim: The golden complex is taxonomically broad and includes species with distant phylogenetic origins.
source: The key members in the golden complex are ants but the complex is taxonomically broad and includes species with distant phylogenetic origins.
evidence: The claim is based on the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The golden complex may include a few other groups, such as bees, flies, and cerambycid beetles, in which some species also have a golden colouration.
source: Beside the species mentioned, it may include a few other groups, such as bees, flies, and cerambycid beetles, in which some species also have a golden colouration.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on observations of other golden-colored species.

claim: The distribution of the majority of the ten putative mimetic rings in the complex overlapped with at least one other ring.
source: The distribution of the majority of the ten putative mimetic rings in the complex overlapped with at least one other ring.
evidence: The claim is based on distribution data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An overlap of golden rings or their non-existence potentially suggests that the variable golden colour patterns produce similar aposematic signals.
source: An overlap of golden rings or actually their non-existence potentially suggests that the variable golden colour patterns produce similar aposematic signals.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the overlap of rings.

claim: Large mimetic complexes include taxa of close and distant phylogenetic origins.
source: Large mimetic complexes include taxa of close and distant phylogenetic origins (e.g., Linsley et al., 1961; Rodriguez et al., 2014) in which the colour pattern is not only a product of common ancestry but also of convergence.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Linsley et al., 1961; Rodriguez et al., 2014.

claim: In large mimetic complexes, the colour pattern is not only a product of common ancestry but also of convergence.
source: Large mimetic complexes include taxa of close and distant phylogenetic origins (e.g., Linsley et al., 1961; Rodriguez et al., 2014) in which the colour pattern is not only a product of common ancestry but also of convergence.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about mimicry complexes.

claim: A shared ancestry is apparent for two species of Myrmarachne spiders.
source: A shared ancestry is apparent for two species of Myrmarachne spiders (Pekár et al., 2017), three species of Daerlac bugs (Casis and Symonds, 2012), and several species of Polyrhachis ants (Robson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pekár et al., 2017.

claim: A shared ancestry is apparent for three species of Daerlac bugs.
source: A shared ancestry is apparent for two species of Myrmarachne spiders (Pekár et al., 2017), three species of Daerlac bugs (Casis and Symonds, 2012), and several species of Polyrhachis ants (Robson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Casis and Symonds, 2012.

claim: A shared ancestry is apparent for several species of Polyrhachis ants.
source: A shared ancestry is apparent for two species of Myrmarachne spiders (Pekár et al., 2017), three species of Daerlac bugs (Casis and Symonds, 2012), and several species of Polyrhachis ants (Robson et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Robson et al., 2015.

claim: The majority of species including Camponotus, Diacamma, Pachycondyla, and Iridomyrmex ants, other spider species, Eurymela treehopers, and Ephutomorpha wasps, have converged on the same phenotype.
source: The majority though, including Camponotus, Diacamma, Pachycondyla, and Iridomyrmex ants, other spider species, Eurymela treehopers, and Ephutomorpha wasps, have converged on the same phenotype as evidenced by their isolation within lineages of non-mimetic colour patterns.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The diversity and geographic pattern of the golden phenotype is likely a result of co-divergence.
source: The diversity and geographic pattern of the golden phenotype is likely a result of co-divergence as found in other complexes (e.g., Rodriguez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on comparison with other complexes.

claim: Species in Müllerian rings described to date use a single defensive trait to teach predators that they are distasteful.
source: Species in Müllerian rings described to date, e.g. heliconid butterflies, use a single defensive trait to teach predators that they are distasteful (e.g., Van Zandt Brower, 1958).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Van Zandt Brower, 1958.

claim: Species in the golden complex use multiple defensive traits including a variety of structural and chemical defences.
source: Species in our golden complex use multiple defensive traits including a variety of structural and chemical defences.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements of defensive traits presented in Table 3.

claim: A thick cuticle is effective against arthropod predators but ineffective against vertebrates.
source: For example, a thick cuticle is effective against arthropod predators but ineffective against vertebrates (Evans and Sanson, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Evans and Sanson, 2005.

claim: Spines are effective against vertebrates but ineffective in the defence against arthropod predators.
source: On the other hand, spines are effective against vertebrates but ineffective in the defence against arthropod predators (Mikolajewski et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mikolajewski et al., 2006.

claim: Some spiders are able to catch ants even with a thick cuticle while others are not.
source: For example, some spiders are able to catch ants even with a thick cuticle while others are not (Pekár and Toft, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pekár and Toft, 2015.

claim: The positive relationship between the index of unpalatability and the response of skinks strongly suggests that the measure is a good proxy for unpalatability.
source: Although our approach is simplistic, the positive relationship between the index of unpalatability and the response of skinks strongly suggests that the measure is a good proxy for unpalatability.
evidence: The claim is based on the correlation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Some of the defensive traits were strongly correlated with body size.
source: Some of the defensive traits were strongly correlated with body size.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analyses of the defensive trait measurements.

claim: Body size alone is an anatomical constraint that may prevent predation.
source: Body size alone is an anatomical constraint that may prevent predation, thus it is difficult to separate the effect of pure body size from the relative size of some defensive traits (e.g., spines).
evidence: The claim is based on general ecological knowledge.

claim: It is the absolute size of defences not their relative size that is ecologically important.
source: It is, however, the absolute size of defences not their relative size that is ecologically important (e.g., a skink will swallow larger spines with greater difficulty than smaller ones).
evidence: The claim is based on logical reasoning about predator-prey interactions.

claim: The golden/black colour combination is somewhat similar to the classic aposematic yellow/black phenotype.
source: Our study describes a new complex with a golden/black colour combination. This combination is somewhat similar to the classic aposematic yellow/black phenotype (Ruxton et al., 2004; Williams, 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with established knowledge about aposematic coloration.

claim: The coverage of golden colour acts as an honest signal of aposematism.
source: Accordingly, our findings support the idea the coverage of golden colour acts as an honest signal of aposematism.
evidence: The claim is based on the positive correlation between golden area and unpalatability.

claim: All the predators in staged trials exhibited an aversion to the prey with the greatest coverage of golden colour.
source: All the predators in staged trials exhibited an aversion to the prey with the greatest coverage of golden colour.
evidence: The claim is based on results from predation trials shown in Figure 6.

claim: Golden individuals were rarely found in the diet of natural populations of predators.
source: Furthermore, golden individuals were rarely found in the diet of natural populations of predators.
evidence: The claim is based on NGS data from field-collected predators shown in Table 2.

claim: Honest signalling is supported by the positive correlation between the extent of the golden colour and unpalatability.
source: Honest signalling is further supported by the positive correlation between the extent of the golden colour and unpalatability, controlling for body size in the analyses via phylogenetic correlation or as a covariate.
evidence: The claim is based on the GLS analysis results.

claim: The theory of honest signalling predicts a relationship between signal and defense within rather than across species.
source: The theory of honest signalling, however, predicts such a relationship within rather than across species.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical expectations from signaling theory.

claim: Recent evidence shows that the relationship between signal and defense can also exist across closely related aposematic species.
source: However, recent evidence shows that this relationship can also exist across closely related aposematic species (Cortesi and Cheney, 2010; María Arenas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cortesi and Cheney, 2010; María Arenas et al., 2015.

claim: Members of the golden complex are defined by a metallic golden sheen.
source: Unlike the classic yellow/black combination, members of the golden complex are defined by a metallic golden sheen.
evidence: The claim is based on visual observations documented in figures.

claim: The golden sheen reflects brightly under direct sunlight making the animals very conspicuous.
source: This sheen reflects brightly under direct sunlight making the animals very conspicuous, at least to a human observer.
evidence: The claim is based on observations by the authors.

claim: In other systems, reflective iridescence has a significant additive effect.
source: In other systems though, reflective iridescence has a significant additive effect (e.g. Fabricant et al., 2014) so it is likely that the sheen enhances the detectability of the signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fabricant et al., 2014.

claim: A possible benefit of the sheen is that it is important for reflecting harmful radiation and dissipating heat.
source: A possible additional benefit, or even an alternative explanation, is that the sheen is important for reflecting harmful radiation and dissipating heat (Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citation to Shi et al., 2015.

claim: The aversion to prey with golden colour was apparent irrespective of the predator's visual sensitivity.
source: The aversion to prey with golden colour was apparent irrespective of the predator's visual sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is based on results from predation trials with different predator types.

claim: Visually- and non-visually orienting predators equally avoided the golden prey.
source: Visually- and non-visually orienting predators equally avoided the golden prey suggesting that golden mimics advertise their unpalatability via multiple sensory modalities.
evidence: The claim is based on results from predation trials shown in Figure 6.

claim: Golden mimics advertise their unpalatability via multiple sensory modalities.
source: Visually- and non-visually orienting predators equally avoided the golden prey suggesting that golden mimics advertise their unpalatability via multiple sensory modalities.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that both visual and non-visual predators avoid mimics.

claim: Some non-visual predators potentially recognize mimics via the patterns of vibrations generated by their movements.
source: Some non-visual predators potentially recognize mimics via the patterns of vibrations generated by their movements (Pekár et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is speculative and supported by citation to Pekár et al., 2011.

claim: Predators typically use multisensory modalities to identify prey.
source: Predators typically use multisensory modalities to identify prey (Bro-Jørgensen, 2010) such as movement, shape and defensive chemicals they emit.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bro-Jørgensen, 2010.

claim: The measure of unpalatability suggested that the highest proportion of individuals was moderately defended.
source: Our measure of unpalatability suggested that the highest proportion of individuals was moderately defended and defensiveness is distributed from highly defended to weakly defended.
evidence: The claim is based on the distribution shown in Figure 4A.

claim: This finding is in agreement with previous claims that mimicry rings are dominated by moderately defended species.
source: This is in agreement with previous claims that mimicry rings are dominated by moderately defended species (Sherratt, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sherratt, 2008.

claim: With a predominance of moderately defended prey, there is an expectation that their presence will erode the effectiveness of the model.
source: With a predominance of moderately defended prey, there is an expectation that their presence will erode the effectiveness of the model.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical expectations from mimicry theory.

claim: All mimics investigated in predator-prey trials experienced significantly lower mortality than the non-mimetic species.
source: Instead, all mimics investigated in our predator-prey trials experienced significantly lower mortality than the non-mimetic species, and this was irrespective of the coverage of gold.
evidence: The claim is based on results from predation trials shown in Figure 6.

claim: Skinks were more likely to attack the lesser-defended individuals.
source: We found the skinks were more likely to attack the lesser-defended individuals but when the suite of predators was taken into account there was little variation in the overall predation pressure.
evidence: The claim is based on results from predation trials.

claim: When the suite of predators was taken into account there was little variation in the overall predation pressure.
source: We found the skinks were more likely to attack the lesser-defended individuals but when the suite of predators was taken into account there was little variation in the overall predation pressure.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Some predators may not use the visual signal as a reference and are cuing in on other signals.
source: This is potentially because some predators may not use the visual signal as a reference and are cuing in on other signals.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the observation that non-visual predators also avoid mimics.

claim: Diet analyses showed predators of all guilds captured mimics with very low frequency.
source: Diet analyses of several potential predators also showed predators of all guilds, including non-visually oriented predators, captured mimics with very low frequency.
evidence: The claim is based on NGS data shown in Table 2.

claim: The predators used in the study are known to feed on non-mimetic prey.
source: The predators that we used are known to feed on non-mimetic prey too (Jackson and Harding, 1982; Daniels, 1987; Platnick, 2000; Higgins et al., 2001; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jackson and Harding, 1982; Daniels, 1987; Platnick, 2000; Higgins et al., 2001; McGinley et al., 2015.

claim: Birds learn to avoid both Müllerian models and mimics irrespective of the availability of alternative prey.
source: However, birds learn to avoid both Müllerian models and mimics irrespective of the availability of alternative prey (Lindström et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lindström et al., 2004.

claim: There are multiple species of ant and ant models distributed across the sampling habitat occupying both terrestrial and arboreal habitats.
source: In addition, there are multiple species of ant and ant models distributed across the sampling habitat occupying both terrestrial and arboreal habitats.
evidence: The claim is based on field observations.

claim: The majority of the species in the complex are ants and ants are typically super abundant due to their sociality.
source: The majority of the species in the complex are also ants and ants are typically super abundant due to their sociality.
evidence: The claim is based on the species composition data and general knowledge about ant ecology.

claim: Mimetic complexes that incorporate a range of different forms of defence are more common than previously believed.
source: We predict that mimetic complexes that incorporate a range of different forms of defence are not only more common than previously believed, but also more likely result in mutualism among the unequally defended members of the complex.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the findings of this study.

claim: Mimetic complexes that incorporate a range of different forms of defence are more likely to result in mutualism among the unequally defended members of the complex.
source: We predict that mimetic complexes that incorporate a range of different forms of defence are not only more common than previously believed, but also more likely result in mutualism among the unequally defended members of the complex.
